A graphical model visualization of the linear model, shown here in case you find it helpful. Shaded circles are observable variables. White circles are latent variables. These are the variables that constitute the degrees of freedom of the model, the paramters that are fit to the data. Diamonds shapes indicate variables that are determined by other variables. The index $i = 1, ..., N$ refers identifies the observations (usually, the rows) in your data. Note that $\sigma$, unlike $\mu_i$ is assuemd to be constant across observations. This is the assumption of the homogeneity of variance, which you might have heard of if you're familiar with $t$-tests or ANOVA.
:::

# The linear model (LM)

LMs (aka linear regression) can be thought of as an example of a much larger
family of regression models that describe an *outcome* variable $y$ (aka the *dependent*
variable) as the function $g$ of one or more *predictor* variables $x_1$, ...,
$x_k$ (aka *independent* variables), $y = g(x_1, ..., x_k)$. In this sense, the
LM is a---very constrained---*predictive model*.[^1] Specifically, the LM assumes
that $y$ is a draw from a Normal distribution $\mathcal{N}$ with constant
standard deviation $\sigma$ and a mean $\mu$ that is a *linear combination* (the
weighted sum) of all the predictors included in the model:

[^1]: While the LM is a specific case of a much wider class of models, it is already 
a rather general model. For example, $t$-tests and analysis of variances (ANOVA) are 
special cases of LMs. We'll return to this point in a later lecture.

\begin{align}
\mathbf{y} & \sim & \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma_{resid}) \\
\mathbf{E}[y] & = & \beta_1 \mathbf{x_1} + ... \beta_k \mathbf{x_k}  \\
    & = & X\beta
\end{align}

Here, $y$ is a column vector of outcome observations of length $n$ (e.g., a
column in your data table), $X$ is is called the $n$ x $k$ *model (or design)
matrix* (e.g., in the simplest case, a number of $k$ columns in your data table)
and $\beta$ is a vector of weight values of length $k$ (aka coefficients)---one
for each of the $k$ predictors in the model. $\mathbf{E}[y]$ refers to the *expected value* of $y$, which is the mean of the Normal distribution from which $y$ is assumed to be drawn.

In the literature, LMs are often written in a number of different ways. For
instance, one might describe the linear model for each observation $i$ of the
outcome $y_i$ and all predictors $x_{1,i}, ..., x_{k,i}$:[^2]

[^2]: $\epsilon_i$ is the *residual* for observation $i$ (= observed $y_i$ -
    predicted $\hat{y_i}$).

\begin{align}
y_i & = & \beta_1x_{1,i}+...+\beta_kx_{k,i} + \epsilon_i, & \ \epsilon_i \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma_{resid}) 
\end{align}

or in vector or matrix form, as in James et al. (2013, p. 63):

\begin{align}
{\mathbf y} & = &  \beta_1{\mathbf x_1}+...+\beta_k{\mathbf x_k} + \epsilon, & \ \epsilon \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma_{resid}) \\
            & = & X\beta + \epsilon,                                         & \ \epsilon \sim \mathrm{Normal}(0, \sigma_{resid}) 
\end{align}

or combining equations (1) and (3) from above, as in Gelman & Hill (2007, p.
38):

\begin{align}
\mathbf{y} & = & \mathrm{Normal}(X\beta, \sigma_{resid}) &  &  & 
\end{align}

Any of these formulations are equivalent, and all are used in the literature. I'm mentioning them here only since it can be confusing as a learner to see these different 
notations. There is no need to memorize them. Finally, a common---but arbitrary---convention is to use a different symbol for
one particular predictor, the *intercept* $\alpha$:

\begin{align}
y   & \sim & \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma) \\
\mu & =    & \alpha + \beta_1 x_1 + ... \beta_k x_k \\
    & =    & \alpha x_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + ... \beta_k x_k
\end{align}

Here, $x_0$ is assumed to be the constant 1, i.e., $x_0 = 1$. This convention
singles out $\alpha$, which helps to realize that it has an intuitive
interpretation: it is the predicted value of the outcome $y$ when all
$x_1 = ... = x_k = 0$.[^3]

[^3]: Depending on how we *code* the predictors $x_1 = ... = x_k = 0$, the intercept can have even conceptually relevant interpretations. For example, if all predictors are centered (so that their means are 0), then the intercept is the predicted sample mean of all $y_i$, $\mathbf{E}[\mathbf{E}[y_i]] = \mathbf{E}[{\mathbf y}]$. We'll learn more about predictor coding in a later lecture.

## Assumptions of the LM

As a theoretical model the LM makes several assumptions (cf. Gelman & Hill,
2007, p. 45). The first two assumptions are shared with many/most other
statistical models we use (to be precise, some models don't strictly make these
assumptions, but they do correct for their violations):

-   **Independence of observations/errors**. Each observation $y$ is assumed to
    be drawn independent of all other observations.
-   **Validity/exhaustivity**.

The other assumptions are more specific to the LM, though the last two of these
are shared with generalized linear model (GLM) and generalized linear mixed-effect 
model (GLMM) that we'll cover in later lectures:[^4]

[^4]: The final two assumptions sometimes confuse learners, and we'll return to 
    them in later lectures. For now, I note that it can be helpful to distinguish between **input variables** and the **predictors**
    we derive from them. For example, in the case study presented below, one *input variable* is $VOT$. But we could include both $VOT$ and $VOT^2$ as
    separate *predictors* in the LM. This would model both linear and quadratic effects
    of VOT, both of which are assumed to have linear effects on the outcome $y$.
    Similarly, we can include interactions of the input variable $VOT$ and some
    other predictor in the model, which will add their product as a predictor to
    the model. That is, we can very much use an LM to ask whether two variables
    interact. The additivity assumption just
    means that the effect of the interaction predictor is assumed to be added
    to the effects of the other predictors in the model.

-   **Normality of errors**. $y$ is drawn from a Normal distribution
    $\mathcal{N}$ (with mean $\mu = X\beta$), and thus is assumed to be able to
    take any real value from $-\infty$ to $+\infty$. Equivalently, we can say
    that the *residuals* (or prediction errors) are drawn from a Normal
    distribution (with mean 0).
-   **Equal variance of errors**. While $\mathrm{E}[y] = \mu$ is assumed to vary
    with the predictors $X$, the residual standard deviation around that mean
    $\sigma$ is assumed to be independent of $X$, and thus constant and
    identical across all observations.
-   **Additivity of effects**. The *effects* of predictors are assumed to be
    additive: $\mathrm{E}[y]$ is assumed to be the weighted *sum* of the
    predictors.
-   **Linearity of each effects**. $y$ is linear in the $\beta$s. That is, the
    *effects* of predictors are assumed to be linear.

Many, if not most, of these assumptions are actually violated when we apply the
model. To some extent linear regression is robust to such violations, depending
on the specific assumption. For example, instead of equality of variance it is
often sufficient that variances are similar (*homogeneity* of variance) or that
the variance-covariance matrix does not exhibit *heteroscedasticity*.[^5] **But
violations of the independence, normality, or homoscedasticity assumptions can
make a model invalid, and the statistical inferences based on it invalid**
(e.g., by inflating Type I and II errors). We return to these points in later
classes.

[^5]: From Ancient Greek [*hetero*---"different" and
    *skedasis*---"dispersion"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heteroscedasticity).
    Homoscedasticity extends the notion of homogeneity of variance to the
    *co*variance between variables

## Use of the LM in our field(s)

While the LM can be used as a predictive model---i.e., to make predictions about unseen data---this is not the primary use of the LMin our fields. Rather, we tend to fit an LM (or other regression models) to the sample of data we have collected, and then conduct statistical inferences about the *effects* of one or more of the model's predictors based on the best-fitting parameterization of that model. Best-fitting parameterization refers to the estimates of $\beta$s (and the residual standard deviation $\sigma$, though we don't tend to be interested in this parameter) that make the LM deliver the best predictions about the observed values of $y$. We'll briefly cover what "best" means in this context in the next section, and we'll return to it in more depth later in the semester.

When we employ an LM during data analysis, we are making the assumption that
this model describes the relation between the predictors and the outcome in the
population we seek to study. This also means that all of our conclusions are
contingent on these assumptions, including in particular the assumption that we
have considered all relevant variables (or have otherwise ruled out that other
effects can confound our analysis).

```{r}
#| label: fig-geometric
#| echo: false
#| column: margin
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "Examples of an LM with one continuous predictor (top; the line) and two continuous predictors (bottom; the plane)."
library(scatterplot3d)

set.seed(42)
n <- 60
d_geo1 <- tibble(x1 = runif(n, 0, 10)) %>%
  mutate(y = 2 + 1.5 * x1 + rnorm(n, 0, 3))
m_geo1 <- lm(y ~ x1, data = d_geo1)

d_geo2 <- tibble(x1 = runif(n, 0, 10), x2 = runif(n, 0, 10)) %>%
  mutate(y = 2 + 1.2 * x1 + 0.8 * x2 + rnorm(n, 0, 2))
m_geo2 <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d_geo2)

par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(d_geo1$x1, d_geo1$y, pch = 16, cex = .7, xlab = expression(x[1]), ylab = "y")
abline(m_geo1, col = "blue")

s3d <- scatterplot3d(d_geo2$x1, d_geo2$x2, d_geo2$y, pch = 16, angle = 55,
                      xlab = expression(x[1]), ylab = expression(x[2]), zlab = "y",
                      color = "black", mar = c(3, 3, 1, 1))
s3d$plane3d(m_geo2, draw_polygon = TRUE, draw_lines = TRUE,
            polygon_args = list(col = adjustcolor("lightblue", alpha.f = .5), border = NA))
```

# Geometric intuitions

Generally speaking, an LM with $k$
predictors (plus the intercept) can be thought of as defining a hyperplane in a
$k+1$ dimensional space, where the additional dimension is the outcome. We'll 
cover this part in more depth in class since it's easier to appreciate on a whiteboard. 
A great introduction with effective visualizations is provided in James et al. (2013, Ch 3)  *Introduction to statistical learning*.

For
instance, for a single predictor, the LM defines a line that describes the
predicted outcome as a function of the single predictor. For two predictors, the
LM defines a plane in the 3D space defined by the two predictors and the
outcome, etc. (for some examples, see @fig-geometric).

## What makes a line fit well? Residuals, RSS, and likelihood

When we look at @fig-geometric, it seems intuitive that the line/hyperplane provides a relatively good fit to the points. But what does that mean and how can we quantify *goodness-of-fit*? Later in the semester, we'll learn different approaches to this question and how they relate to each other. For now, here's a brief primer in case you're curious, but don't worry if it doesn't yet all make sense.

We illustrate this here for the
single-predictor case, since it is the easiest to draw. There are two related
but distinct ideas: (1) a line fits better the smaller its (squared) residuals
are, and (2) a line fits better the higher the *likelihood* of the observed data
is under the normal-error assumption of the LM. It turns out that, for LMs, the two approaches are identical and yield the same best-fitting model. 

**Residuals and the residual sum of squares (RSS).** For any candidate line
$\hat{y}_i = \hat{\alpha} + \hat{\beta}x_i$, the residual for observation $i$ is
the vertical distance between the predicted and the actual outcome, $y_i - \hat{y}_i$ (the red lines below). Squaring and
summing these residuals gives the residual sum of squares,
$RSS = \sum_i (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2$, an intuitive measure of how 'off' the model's predictions are. The three panels below show the same data
with three different hypothetical lines: the actual best (least-squares) fit,
a line with the same slope but shifted down, and a line with the (best-fitting)
intercept but a different slope. Both of the latter two lines fit clearly worse
(larger red residuals, larger RSS) than the best-fitting line. The best-fitting line is the one that minimizes the RSS.

**Likelihood under the normal-error assumption.** Recall that the LM assumes
$y_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\hat\alpha + \hat\beta x_i, \hat\sigma)$: for every value
of $x$, the model places an *identical-variance* normal distribution around the
predicted value $\hat{y}$. The fourth panel below visualizes this by drawing a
few of these normal distributions (in red), rotated so that they sit vertically
on top of the fit line. For a few example points, the annotated value is the
*log-density* of that point's observed $y_i$ under its corresponding normal
distribution, $\log p(y_i \mid \hat\alpha, \hat\beta)$---points close to the line
fall in the peak of the density (higher, i.e., less negative log-density) than
points far from the line. Summing the log-densities across all observations
gives the (log-)likelihood of the data under the fitted line,
$\Lambda = \sum_i \log p(y_i \mid \hat\alpha, \hat\beta)$. It turns out that,
for the LM, choosing $\hat\alpha, \hat\beta$ to maximize $\Lambda$---maximizing the model's likelihood---is the *same* as minimizing the RSS---minimzing the summed (squared) prediction error!

```{r rss-likelihood-setup, echo=FALSE}
library(ggrepel)

set.seed(123)
n_rss <- 20
d_rss <- tibble(x = runif(n_rss, 0, 10)) %>%
  mutate(y = 3 + 1.5 * x + rnorm(n_rss, 0, 2.5))
m_rss <- lm(y ~ x, data = d_rss)
alpha_hat <- coef(m_rss)[1]
beta_hat  <- coef(m_rss)[2]
sigma_hat <- sigma(m_rss)

base_size <- 11 * 1.15
x_curve <- seq(1, 9, length.out = 5)
scale_dens <- 3

# Panel showing one hypothetical line, its residuals, and the resulting RSS
plot_line_and_rss <- function(alpha, beta, title, bold = FALSE) {
  d <- d_rss %>% mutate(yhat = alpha + beta * x)
  rss <- sum((d$y - d$yhat)^2)
  lab <- paste(deparse(bquote(
    RSS == sum((y[i] - hat(y)[i])^2, i == 1, n) ~ "=" ~ .(round(rss, 1)))),
    collapse = " ")

  ggplot(d, aes(x, y)) +
    geom_segment(aes(xend = x, yend = yhat), color = "red", linewidth = .4) +
    geom_abline(intercept = alpha, slope = beta, color = "blue") +
    geom_point(size = 1.5) +
    annotate("text", x = min(d$x), y = max(d$y) + 1, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
             color = "red", size = 3.45, fontface = if (bold) "bold" else "plain",
             parse = TRUE, label = lab) +
    labs(title = title, x = "x", y = "y") +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    theme_bw(base_size = base_size)
}

# Panel showing normal distributions (in red) centered vertically on the same line
plot_line_and_loglik <- function(alpha, beta, bold = FALSE) {
  curve_df <- map_dfr(x_curve, function(xc) {
    yhat_c <- alpha + beta * xc
    ygrid <- seq(yhat_c - 3.5 * sigma_hat, yhat_c + 3.5 * sigma_hat, length.out = 200)
    tibble(x = xc + dnorm(ygrid, mean = yhat_c, sd = sigma_hat) * scale_dens,
           y = ygrid, group = xc)
  })

  set.seed(1)
  d_ann <- d_rss %>%
    mutate(yhat = alpha + beta * x,
           logdens = dnorm(y, yhat, sigma_hat, log = TRUE)) %>%
    slice(sample(seq_len(n_rss), 4)) %>%
    mutate(lab = map_chr(logdens, ~ paste(
      deparse(bquote(log * p == .(round(.x, 2)))), collapse = " ")))

  loglik <- sum(dnorm(d_rss$y, alpha + beta * d_rss$x, sigma_hat, log = TRUE))
  lab_loglik <- paste(deparse(bquote(
    Lambda == sum(log * p(y[i] * "|" * hat(alpha) * "," * hat(beta)), i == 1, n) ~ "=" ~ .(round(loglik, 1)))),
    collapse = " ")

  ggplot() +
    geom_abline(intercept = alpha, slope = beta, color = "blue") +
    geom_point(data = d_rss, aes(x, y), size = 1.5) +
    geom_path(data = curve_df, aes(x, y, group = group), color = "red") +
    geom_point(data = d_ann, aes(x, y), color = "red", size = 1.5) +
    geom_text_repel(data = d_ann, aes(x, y, label = lab), parse = TRUE,
              color = "red", size = 3.105, seed = 1,
              segment.color = NA, max.overlaps = Inf, min.segment.length = Inf) +
    annotate("text", x = .3, y = max(d_rss$y) + 2, hjust = 0, vjust = 1,
             color = "red", size = 3.68, fontface = if (bold) "bold" else "plain",
             parse = TRUE, label = lab_loglik) +
    labs(x = "x", y = "y") +
    coord_cartesian(clip = "off") +
    theme_bw(base_size = base_size)
}

p_best_rss        <- plot_line_and_rss(alpha_hat, beta_hat, "Best fit", bold = TRUE)
p_best_loglik     <- plot_line_and_loglik(alpha_hat, beta_hat, bold = TRUE)
p_shifted_rss     <- plot_line_and_rss(alpha_hat - 8, beta_hat, "Shifted down (same slope)")
p_shifted_loglik  <- plot_line_and_loglik(alpha_hat - 8, beta_hat)
p_slope_rss       <- plot_line_and_rss(alpha_hat, beta_hat - 1.2, "Different slope")
p_slope_loglik    <- plot_line_and_loglik(alpha_hat, beta_hat - 1.2)
```

```{r rss-likelihood-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=10, fig.cap="Three hypothetical lines for the same data (rows), with the resulting residuals and RSS (left column) and the corresponding normal-likelihood visualization (right column). Points colored in red (right column) are the ones for which the log-density is annotated. The best-fitting line (top row, boldface summary) has the smallest RSS and the highest log-likelihood of the three."}
(p_best_rss | p_best_loglik) /
  (p_shifted_rss | p_shifted_loglik) /
  (p_slope_rss | p_slope_loglik)
```

# General workflow

```{r}
# download.file(
#   url = "https://github.com/hlplab/constraints-on-distributional-learning-VOT/blob/main/data/experiment-results.csv",
#   destfile = "../data/Tan-Jaeger.csv")

d <- 
  read.csv("../data/Tan-Jaeger.csv") %>%
  # Remove catch trials
  filter(!is.na(Response.Voicing)) %>%
  # Some variable typing
  mutate(
    across(c(ParticipantID, Block, Condition.Exposure), factor),
    Response.t = ifelse(Response.Voicing == "voiceless", 1, 0)) %>%
  rename(VOT = Item.VOT, Condition = Condition.Exposure) %>%
  # making response variable a little easier to understand for non-language scientists
  mutate(Response.isT = ifelse(Response.Voicing == "voiceless", T, F)) 
```

Here's the general workflow I'd recommend for an LM analysis, following adequate
data checks, variable typing (e.g., making sure that variables that are factors
indeed are factors, etc.) and filtering (e.g., removal of practice and/or catch
trials, outlier exclusion, etc.). Some of these steps won't yet make sense since 
they refer to concepts we have not yet covered. I mention them here so that you 
can use this workflow section as a general recipe to look up later.

-   Get data into table format, with each observation of your data corresponding
    to one row of the table and separate columns for the outcome and each of the
    input variables. What counts as an observation depends on the question you 
    intend to ask.

-   Decide whether to transform your continuous input variables,
    e.g., by centering and/or standardizing them. Decide how to code the factors in your data, so that each of the factor
    input variables can be translated into one ore more numerical
    predictors. We'll cover how to code categorical predictors in a separate
    lecture. For now, I'll note that most statistics packages will 
    quietly apply default coding if you do not specify it yourself. 
    Since the interpretation of the regression output depends on the specific predictor coding, this is something that you should always keep in mind.

-   Define the regression formula $y \sim 1 + x_1 + ... + x_k$, **where 1 stands
    for the constant 1**. Together with the data table and information about the
    factor coding (which is stored as an attribute to the factor column in the
    data.frame in R and in many similar programs), this formula contains all the
    information that is required for a function intended to fit the model to the
    data.

    A call to the LM-fitting function typically first implicitly creates the
    model matrix $X$. **Looking at the model matrix corresponding to an LM or
    other model can be a very effective way to learn to understand formula
    syntax in whatever language you're using.** By default, this model matrix
    will contain the constant 1 as the first column, followed by one column per
    *predictor*. Note that this can be more columns than the number of input
    variables. For example, factor input variables with $k$ distinct levels will
    result in $k-1$ distinct predictors, and thus $k-1$ distinct columns in the
    model matrix. Similarly, interactions in the formula add additional columns
    to the model matrix (more on that in a later lecture). And there are a
    number of other common formula abbreviations that will expand into multiple
    columns in the design matrix. If you're not sure what a formula does, I
    recommend simply looking at the model matrix it creates (in R, `model.matrix(lm(...))`):

```{r model-matrix, echo=FALSE}
model.matrix(
  lm(data = d, formula = Response.RT ~ 1 + Condition * VOT)) %>%
  # Select 20 random rows from the model matrix for illustration
  as_tibble() %>% 
  slice_sample(n = 15)
```

Note that the formula that we use to define our LM contains only all the *known*
or *observable* variables, both the outcome variable and the input variables.
The *unknown latent* variables---the $\beta$s and $\sigma$---are not mentioned
in the formula. That's because those are the variables we're asking to be
*estimated*, e.g., one $\beta$ for each predictor. The estimates that we get
from fitting the LM are what is reported in the output of the LM if you print or
summarize it.

# Working through an example

Next, we'll go through an example. We'll use the data from [Tan & Jaeger (2025).
*Learning to understand an unfamiliar talker: Testing distributional learning as a model of rapid adaptive speech perception*](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0010027725001350).
The data come from an experiment on adaptive speech perception, and contain both
responses and reaction times from a two-alternative forced-choice task (2AFC).
From the abstract of Tan & Jaeger:

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-trial
#| column: margin
#| fig-width: 3
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: "The same simple 2AFC task on all trials. Participants started each trial by clicking the green button. A recording played, and **participants had to answer which of the two words they heard**."
knitr::include_graphics("figures/trial_example.png")
```

> [...] a few minutes of exposure can significantly reduce the processing
> difficulty listeners experience during initial encounters with an unfamiliar
> accent. How such adaptation unfolds incrementally, however, remains largely
> unknown, leaving basic predictions by theories of adaptive speech perception
> untested. [...] We begin to address these knowledge gaps in a novel
> incremental exposure-test paradigm. We expose US English listeners to shifted
> phonetic distributions of word-initial stops (e.g., "dill" vs. "till"), while
> incrementally assessing cumulative changes in listeners' perception. [...]

The following figure illustrates the design of the study, consisting of three
between-participant exposure conditions, crossed with nine within-participant
blocks, each eliciting responses along the phonetic VOT continuum (measured at
12 points). VOT refers to voice onset timing, and is the primary cue to the
contrasts like *dip* and *tip* in US English. It is the time between the opening
of a speaker's lips (release the air burst) and the start of vocal fold
vibrations. As little as 5ms difference in that time can make the difference
between hearing the word *dip* (lower VOT) and the word *tip* (higher VOT). The
three between-participant condition differed only in the distribution of VOT
during exposure blocks.

```{r}
#| column: page
#| fig-cap: 'Incremental exposure-test design. Histograms summarize distribution of voice onset time (VOT) in each block (dark bars: "d"-words; light: "t"-words). The three *between-participant* conditions (rows) differed only in the distribution of VOT during exposure blocks. VOTs in test blocks were identical within & across conditions.'
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| cache: true
#| out-width: '100%'
knitr::include_graphics("figures/block_design.png")
```

Specifically, the green condition has the exact same distribution as the red
condition, but shifted 10ms to the right; the blue condition is shifted +40ms to
the right. This design makes it possible to assess how participants'
interpretation of the same physical VOT input during the gray test blocks
changes as a function of the differently shifted VOT distributions during the
exposure blocks. **This makes it possible to test whether listeners change their
categorization functions over VOT as a function of recent input from a talker**.

121 participants were included for analysis, each providing 144 exposure trials
(3 blocks) and 72 test trials (6 blocks). Participants were unaware of the
exposure-test structure of the experiment, and the procedure for exposure and
test trials was identical: participants saw two words on the screen (e.g., "dip"
and "tip"). Participants then heard a recording of a single word and then had to
click the word they heard. All recordings were spoken by the same voice. Here
**we use only the data from the six gray test blocks**, leaving `r nrow(d)`
observations.

## The data

Since we want to avoid violations of the assumption of independence, we use the
data from a single participant from the Shift40 condition, leaving us with
$6 * 12 = 72$ observations. Here's some of the data of that participant. If you
downloaded this R markdown document, feel free to change the participant, and
see how that changes the results.

```{r}
dd <- 
  d %>% 
  filter(
    Condition == "Shift40",
    Phase == "test") %>%
  filter(ParticipantID == first(ParticipantID)) %>%
  # select only the columns of the data that are relevant for this tutorial
  select(ParticipantID, Condition, Phase, Block, Trial, VOT, Response.isT, Response.RT) 

head(dd, 15)
```

## Example 1: Analyzing the effects of VOT on response times

We'll begin by analyzing the effects of VOT on response RTs. This makes response
RTs our outcome variable, and VOTs the input variable. The first decision we
need to make is how we'd like to code VOT. For example, we could treat VOT as a
continuous predictor or as a factor with 12 distinct levels (the number of
measurement locations along VOT). And, if we treat VOT as a continuous
predictor, we could include only linear VOT or also quadratic VOT or higher
order polynomials, provided we have enough data to avoid overfitting.[^8]
Similarly, we could decide to include log-transformed VOT instead of VOT, or
other transforms. As described above, the linearity assumption of LMs does not
prevent us from applying non-linear transform to any of the input variables.

[^8]: As a rule of thumb, the number of coefficients in the LM should be less
    than 1/20th of the number of data points, $k < n / 20$. But that's just a
    rule of thumb, and details depend on how balanced the data is with regard to
    the distribution of predictor values.

For the present example, we will treat VOT as a continuous predictor and only
include its linear component.[^9] 

[^9]: When we treat a predictor $x$ as continuous, we making the assumption that
    a change in its value of 1 unit has the same effect on the outcome $y$,
    regardless of where along $x$ that change is added. That follows from the
    linearity assumption mentioned above.

A second decision we need to make---not necessarily in this order---is what statistical 
framework to use. For example, we could use a frequentist framework or we could use a 
Bayesian framework. If you've never heard about these frameworks, I recommend 
reading Ch 1 of Gelman et al. 2025 ("Regressions and other stories"). It provides a *very*
concise, high-level and neutral overview of these two ways of thinking about statistics. 
There is a lot of decisions hidden in the choice of framework, and the choice does have 
consequences for how we fit the model. The choice between these 
frameworks also *can*, but doesn't necessarily always, affect the conclusions we would draw 
from our analysis. That is why we will revisit the distinction between frequentist and 
Bayesian statistics later in the semester. 

For now, here's a frequentist LM. The R function `lm` automatically fits to the model with 
the specified formula to the data `dd`:

```{r, echo=T}
lm.frequentist <- lm(formula = Response.RT ~ 1 + VOT, data = dd)
print(lm.frequentist)
```

This basic output, which shows the best-fitting parameter estimates for the intercept, $\hat{\alpha}$, and the slope of VOT, $\hat{\beta}$, looks almost identical if we instead look at a Bayesian LM.[^priors] Both outputs, also start with a brief summary of what type of model we fit (an LM, which assumes gaussian/normally-distributed residuals) and what formula 
we used:

[^priors]: These estimates were obtained using `stan_glm`'s (weakly informative) 
    default priors, which have little influence on the posterior distribution of 
    the parameters, and help avoid overfitting. If that all sounds like gibberish 
    to you, don't fret. We'll cover priors and Bayesian statistics in later lectures. 

```{r, echo=T, results='asis'}
lm.bayesian <- stan_glm(formula = Response.RT ~ 1 + VOT, data = dd)
print(lm.bayesian)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Using this method since stan_glm prints through the C++ stdout, which knitr doesn't capture
# (this isn't an issue when working with stan_glm in the console).
cat(capture.output(print(lm.bayesian)), sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
#| column: margin
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "For the present example, the frequentist and Bayesian LM yield similar estimates, and make very similar predictions. The plots show the predicted response RTs as a function of VOT, with 95% confidence intervals (frequentist) or credible intervals. Points show the data."
#| label: fig-lm-predictions
p.frequentist <- plot_predictions(lm.frequentist, by = "VOT") + xlab("VOT (ms)") + ylab("Response RT (ms)") + ggtitle("Frequentist LM") + geom_point(data = dd, aes(x = VOT, y = Response.RT), size = .1, color = "black", alpha = .5)
p.bayesian <- plot_predictions(lm.bayesian, by = "VOT") + xlab("VOT (ms)") + ylab("Response RT (ms)") + ggtitle("Bayesian LM") + geom_point(data = dd, aes(x = VOT, y = Response.RT), size = .1, color = "black", alpha = .5)

p.frequentist /
 p.bayesian
```

The specific output will depend on the package you use. For this particular set of functions, the default output of the Bayesian `stan_glm` function is a bit more verbose; it also prints, for instance, the estimate of the residual standard deviation, $\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon$. This information is also present in the frequentist model; it just wasn't plotted as part of the default output:

```{r, echo=TRUE}
sigma(lm.frequentist)
```

While the estimates of the two models aren't exactly identical, they are quite similar for this example (see also @fig-lm-predictions). This won't always be the case. In later lectures, we'll cover how the choice 
of prior for Bayesian models affects the outcomes, why this is sometimes used to criticize Bayesian statistics, and why this criticism can be misguided. For now, we'll focus on the frequentist LM output, which is likely more familiar. We can obtain more information about the fitted model by summarizing it:


```{r, echo=T}
summary(lm.frequentist)
```

This output can be split into four parts. At the top, the model call is
repeated, which is convenient, for example, when we look at a stored model
object that we created some time ago. Below it, we see a statistical summary of
the residuals.[^10] This summary can be helpful in identifying violations of the
assumption of normality. Here, for example, there is clear summary that the
residuals are *not* normally distributed: the minimum/maximum and quantiles are
not symmetrical around zero. This is to be expected---but often ignored---for
RTs, which are known to be right-skewed with heavy right tails (due to the
boundedness of RTs).[^11]

[^10]: Recall that *residuals* are the prediction error of the LM, the difference between
    the actual and the predicted outcome. Each row of the model matrix $X$
    corresponds to a prediction for that row, and thus has a corresponding
    residual $\epsilon$.

[^11]: For review and large-scale statistical simulations that assess the
    consequences of using LMs and its repeated-measures extension LMMs for the
    analysis of RTs, see Burchill & Jaeger (2024) in *JML*.

The third part of the output summarizes the coefficient estimates
($\hat{\beta}$), their standard errors, the resulting $t$-statistic, and its
$p$-value. The $t$-statistics is a signed measure of the estimates distance from
0 in terms of its own standard error
($t = \frac{\hat{\beta}}{SE_{\hat{\beta}}}$).[^12] The $p$-value is the result
of a Student's $t$-test with the residual DFs of the LM as DFs for the test.
E.g., for the effect of VOT, $t(70) = `r signif(coef(summary(lm.frequentist))[2,3], 4)`$. And if we look
the probability density function for the Student $t$ distribution to ask how
probable this $t$-value is for DF = 70, we'll get
`r signif(pt(q = abs(coef(summary(lm.frequentist))[2,3]), df = lm.frequentist$df.residual, lower.tail = F) * 2, 4)`, 
matching the $p$-value reported in the LM for the effect of VOT.

[^12]: This is just the [standard definition of a
    $t$-value](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T-statistic) as a measure of how
    different an estimate is from some target value. Here, the target value is 0
    since we want to know whether the coefficient for a predictor is different
    from 0. If it is, we say that the predictor "has an effect" on the
    outcome.

Finally, the bottom part of the LM output provides multiple measures of the
goodness of fit of the LM. Of these, the $R^2$ tells us how much of the variance
in the outcome $y$ is accounted for by the model (*for this sample*). Notably,
an LM can have one or more statistically significant effects even if the model
overall accounts for very little variance in out observed outcome. 
The $F$-statistic (here $F(1, 70) = 2.779$) tests whether the
predictors included in the model *together* provide for a statistically
significantly better fit, compared to an LM with just the intercept (the "null
model"). The DFs for this test will always be the number of predictors in the
model. We will return to this $F$-test when we talk about model comparison.

### Write-up

For this particular example, there isn't much to report. Note that we wouldn't
usually care about the intercept, and rarely report it. So we might write:

\color{lightgray}

> To test our hypothesis, we used linear regression to regress the participant's
> reaction time against VOT. The effect of VOT was not significant
> ($\hat{\beta} = -7.6$, $t = -1.67$, $p \geq .1$).

\color{black}

A few considerations:

-   I recommend you provide both the relevant statistics (coefficient estimates,
    $p$-values, etc.), and a descriptive interpretation of that result in
    non-technical language---but we careful to avoid language that is wrong.
-   **Use** $\widehat{\beta}$ when we describe coefficient estimates and write
    up results. This emphasizes that these are *estimates* of the assumed
    population parameters ($\beta$).
-   Try to resist language that suggests significance even when it was not
    found, as in "... did not reach significance".
-   Do not take $p$-values to indicate effect strength. It is ok to write things
    like "highly significant effect" but that is not the same as a "large
    effect". Similarly, a "large effect"---in whatever way that is
    determined---is not necessarily the same a "theoretically particularly
    important" effect.

### Questions to ponder in class

-   How would you interpret the above output?
-   How would we expect the output to change if we centered VOT by subtracting
    the mean VOT from each VOT value before entering it into the model? Which
    estimates of the model would change? Which ones would stay the same?
-   How about if we also standardized VOT (by dividing it by its standard
    deviation)?
-   How could we test whether the slope of VOT changes across Blocks?

Bonus question:

-   How could we test a somewhat more interesting hypothesis that more ambiguous
    VOTs---VOTs that are more likely to elicit an equal proportion of "d"- and
    "t"-responses---are responded to more slowly?

```{r, include=FALSE}
# One possible approach:

# determine ambiguity of VOT by fitting logistic regression to "d"/"t"-responses
# and get negative absolute log-odds as a measure of how ambiguous the token each 
# token is
dd$VOT_ambiguity <- -abs(predict(glm(Response.isT ~ 1 + poly(VOT, 2), data = dd)))

# Use that measure as a predictor of RTs
m <- lm(formula = Response.RT ~ 1 + VOT_ambiguity, data = dd)
summary(m)

# Alternatively, one could just hope that the ambiguous points are roughly in the 
# middle of the continuum, and test whether there is a negative quadratic effect 
# of VOT, but this approach makes far stronger assumptions that might not be (and 
# likely are not) justified.
m <- lm(formula = Response.RT ~ 1 + poly(VOT, 2), data = dd)
summary(m)
```

## A Bayesian LM
Finally, let's return to the Bayesian LM we fit above. We can summarize it in
the same way as we did for the frequentist LM:

```{r, echo=T}
summary(lm.bayesian)
```

Again, the first part summarizes the model we fit, the data we fit it to, and
some information about how the model was fit. The second part provides
estimates of the coefficients, and their standard errors (= the standard
deviation of the estimates). Unlike the frequentist model, the Bayesian LM does
not provide a $t$-statistic or a $p$-value based on that statistic. In fact, we
don't need either of these parametric summaries of the uncertainty we should
maintain about the estimate. That's because the model represents this
uncertainty in the 4000 posterior samples it has drawn from the posterior
distribution of the three parameters of the LM. The quantiles of these
posterior samples are summarized in the output of the LM.[^13] These are the
posterior samples that we can use to test hypotheses about the parameters of
the model, e.g., by asking how many of the posterior samples are above or below
0. For example, we can ask whether RTs decrease with increasing VOT, i.e.,
whether the coefficient for VOT is negative:

[^13]: Note one interesting difference between the Bayesian and frequentist LM
    that we'll return to in later lectures: in the frequentist LM, estimate of
    the standard deviation of the residuals $\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon$ is a point
    estimate---when we obtained `sigma(lm.frequentist)` above, there was no
    uncertainty associated with that estimate, unlike for the estimates of the
    intercept and slope of VOT. This is different in the Bayesian LM, in which
    we obtain the full posterior distribution of $\sigma_\epsilon$ (summarized
    in terms of its quantiles in the output). Bayesians maintain uncertainty
    about *all* parameters in the model.

```{r,echo=T}
hypothesis(lm.bayesian, "VOT < 0")
```

In this case, the hypothesis test tells us that the mean estimate is indeed
negative and that and that 95% of the posterior samples are below 0. We also
see an evidence ratio---essentially a Bayes Factor, about which we'll learn
more later. This evidence ration tells us the odds that a random posterior
sample of the 4000 samples in the fitted model supports the hypothesis we
tested. For the present example, these odds are roughly 17.9-to-1. Based on
common conventions, we might summarize that the evidence for a negative effect
is "moderate", though some Bayesian would prefer not to use *any* dichotomizing
language like that.

The final part of the Bayesian LM summary contains a number of diagnostics. We
won't cover them for now, but the fact that the Rhat's are all very close to 1
indicates that the model has converged and that we have no evidence that the
posterior samples contained in the fitted model don't reflect the posterior
distribution.
